meta.title: Freefall Simulator
meta.description: See how body position changes a skydiver's flight in freefall.

freefall.intro: The skydiver below is you in freefall. How do you want them to fly? Choose wisely.
freefall.sceneLabel: Animation of a skydiver in freefall, belly to earth, seen from the side.

explain.neutral: Neutral box position: hips down, arms and legs symmetrical. The air pushes evenly on your body, so you fall stable without moving.
explain.legsStretch: Legs stretched: the air pushes your legs up, your head drops and you move forward.
explain.legsTuck: Legs tucked: your legs leave the airflow, your back tilts and you slide backward.
explain.armsForward: Arms forward: the air pushes the front of your body up and you slide backward.
explain.armsBack: Arms pulled back: the front of your body catches less air, your head drops and you move forward.
explain.archMore: More arch: your body is more stable and has less drag, so you fall faster.
explain.archFlat: No arch: more area against the air, so you fall slower, but you are less stable and may rock.
explain.dipLeft: Left shoulder down: air spills off your left side and you turn left.
explain.dipRight: Right shoulder down: air spills off your right side and you turn right.

freefall.disclaimer: This animation is a learning aid to help you understand how freefall works. Trust your instructor, and always take your questions to them.

combos.moreArea: Result: more of your body is exposed to the wind, which slows your fall a little. To slow down more, you can also reduce your arch (de-arch).
combos.slowFall: This position is used to slow your fall rate. You can also turn your face to the side, which slows the fall rate a little more.

meta.title: Navigation simulator
meta.description: Plan and fly the landing pattern: holding area, points A, B and C, and landing on target.

navigation.intro: You have just opened your canopy and have checked that it is properly inflated, in a rectangular shape and controllable. You look at your altimeter and you can see you are at 3,000 ft. Plan your navigation, then fly it down to a landing close to the target you planned. Use the two buttons to turn, or click the map to look around.

plan.title: 1. Plan your pattern
plan.seta: The seta on the ground points the landing direction, into the wind.
plan.choose: Tap one of the numbered options on the map.

why.H: The holding area is in the direction the seta points, beyond the target, on the side the wind comes from. That way, even as the wind carries you, you reach point A with height to spare.
why.A: Point A is where the pattern starts, and we should pass over it at 1,000 ft. To reach point A (from the holding area), and to go from A to B, we always fly with a tailwind (the wind behind us).
why.B: Point B (600 ft) is the second point of the pattern, still on the right of the landing line. There you turn left toward point C, and fly with a crosswind.
why.C: Point C (300 ft) is on the landing line, before the target. There you make the last left turn and fly the final approach into the wind to the target.

hints.downwind: Not yet. The seta points into the wind: the holding area and the start of the pattern are on the side the seta points to.
hints.rightSide: Not yet. Every turn in the pattern is to the left: leaving the holding area toward point A, the landing line is always on your left, and the pattern on its right.
hints.both: Not yet. That point is on the wrong side and at the wrong end. Follow the seta, and remember the turns are to the left.
hints.pastTarget: Not yet. From point C you fly the final into the wind to the target, so point C is before the target, on the side the wind comes from.
hints.cRight: Not yet. At point B you turn left, and point C lines up with the target, on the final approach.
hints.holdingSide: Not yet. The holding area is in the direction the seta points, beyond the target.

plan.ready: Plan complete and correct! Time to fly it.
plan.mapLabel: Top-down map of the landing area, seen from 3,000 ft.

flight.title: 2. Navigate to the target
flight.sceneLabel: View from under the canopy, looking forward and down.
flight.holdHint: Hold Left or Right to turn; let go to fly straight. Hold Flare from when the top of the flags around the target (8 ft) is level with your feet until touchdown. Drag the view to look around.

settings.title: Settings
settings.guides: Points A, B and C in flight

report.title: 3. Landing report
report.reached: you passed {dist} m from it, at {alt} ft.
report.far: you passed {dist} m from it, at {alt} ft. The goal is within 30 m of the point.
report.notNear: you weren't near it at the right height (between {low} and {high} ft).

rightTurns.zero: Only left turns during the pattern. Great!
rightTurns.one: {count} 90° right turn after point A. In the pattern, every turn is to the left (small corrections to the right are fine).
rightTurns.other: {count} 90° right turns after point A. In the pattern, every turn is to the left (small corrections to the right are fine).

lowTurns.zero: No sharp turns below 300 ft. Great!
lowTurns.one: {count} sharp turn below 300 ft. A turn close to the ground makes the canopy dive and speed up, and takes away your ability to flare well, greatly increasing the risk of an accident on landing. Below 300 ft, only small corrections.
lowTurns.other: {count} sharp turns below 300 ft. A turn close to the ground makes the canopy dive and speed up, and takes away your ability to flare well, greatly increasing the risk of an accident on landing. Below 300 ft, only small corrections.

flare.high: Flare too early, at {alt} ft. Flare at about 6 to 7 ft (roughly a person's height), when the top of the flags around the target is level with your feet.
flare.low: Flare too late, at {alt} ft. Flare at about 6 to 7 ft (roughly a person's height), when the top of the flags around the target is level with your feet.
flare.none: You didn't flare. Remember to flare at about 6 to 7 ft (roughly a person's height), when the top of the flags around the target is level with your feet.
flare.released: You let go of the flare before touching down. Remember that once you start the flare, you hold it until you touch the ground (even if you started it higher).

landing.legendary: Legendary! You landed {dist} m from the target.
landing.great: Great landing: {dist} m from the target.
landing.goal: Good landing: {dist} m from the target, within the 20 m goal.
landing.missed: You landed {dist} m from the target. The goal is within 20 m.

report.praise: Even with things to improve, you landed close to the target. Well done!
report.clean: A perfect pattern: every point, left turns only, and the flare on time!
report.tip: Tip: start each turn a little before the point, and let go once you line up with the next leg.

story.title: Your landing, as a story
story.alt: Your landing report as an Instagram story: the landing grade, the pattern seen from above and the highlights.
story.hint: On a phone, tap Share and pick Instagram › Story. If it isn't there, download the image and add it to your story from your gallery.
story.shareFailed: Couldn't share from here. Download the image and add it to your story from your gallery.

points.all: Hit points A, B and C

flare.released: Let go of the flare too soon

meta.title: Traveling with your parachute
meta.description: How to take your skydiving rig on a plane: carry-on or checked, the AAD (CYPRES, Vigil, MarS M2) in the X-ray, documents to print and what to say at security.

travel.heading: Traveling with your own parachute on a commercial flight
travel.intro: Carry-on or checked bag, the AAD (Automatic Activation Device) in the X-ray, the papers you should print and what to say when the security officer gives your backpack a funny look.

summary.1: A parachute is **not a prohibited item** in Brazil (ANAC) or in the US (TSA), with or without an AAD, carried on or checked.
summary.2: Prefer to take it **as carry-on**, in a backpack just for the rig.
summary.3: **Print the X-ray card** of your AAD (CYPRES, Vigil or MarS M2) and the manufacturer's statements.
summary.4: **Arrive early.** Screening can take a while, and you need to be there if they open the rig.
summary.5: Nobody should pull any handle. If it has to be opened, **you stay with it and help**.
summary.title: Quick summary

toc.title: On this page
toc.can: Can you take a parachute on a plane?
toc.aad: The AAD in the X-ray: cutter and battery

can.title: 1. Can you take a parachute on a plane?

brazil.1: ANAC's [Informativo SIA 29/20](https://www.gov.br/anac/pt-br/centrais-de-conteudo/aeroportos-e-aerodromos/informativos-sia/2020-29) (in Portuguese) covers exactly this. The list of items prohibited in departure areas (Annex 1 of ANAC Resolution 515/2019) **does not include parachute equipment**. So, from an aviation security point of view, it can go as carry-on.
brazil.2: The notice also says what to expect:
brazil.title: In Brazil (ANAC)

list.1: The X-ray image may raise questions, because airport security staff almost never see a parachute.
list.2: If they think it necessary, they may use the explosive trace detector or search it by hand.
list.3: For a hand search, **the passenger must be present**, whether the bag is carried on or checked.
list.4: That's why ANAC recommends getting to the airport **as early as possible**.

usa.title: In the United States (TSA)
usa.text: According to [USPA](https://www.uspa.org/traveling-with-equipment), the TSA has national guidance for its officers: parachutes are allowed **carried on and checked, with or without an AAD**. Officers may not touch or pull the handles, or force the rig open. If it has to be opened, the owner must be present, may help, and may repack it afterwards.

can.airline: **Note:** the authorities allow it, but **the airline may have its own rules** (usually on weight, size and excess baggage). Check your airline's rules before you travel.

bags.title: 2. Carry-on or checked?
bags.text: Both are allowed, but the general advice is to **carry it on**.

cabin.1: The rig never leaves your side.
cabin.2: No risk of it getting lost, knocked around or soaked by someone else's bag.
cabin.3: If they need to inspect it, you're already there.
cabin.4: Use a backpack just for the rig and **put nothing else in it**: other objects make the X-ray image harder to read.
cabin.title: Carry-on (recommended)

checked.1: Use a dedicated bag. Helmet and jumpsuit can go with it.
checked.2: Leave the **AAD card on top** of the rig.
checked.3: If the bag sets off an alert, security pages you over the speakers. **Stay near check-in** for about 30 to 45 minutes after dropping it off.
checked.4: In the US, if the TSA can't find you, the rig **doesn't fly**.
checked.5: The airline's liability limit is far below what a rig is worth.
checked.title: Checked

remove.title: What to take out of the carry-on
remove.text: USPA lists items that draw attention in the X-ray and are better checked, if you can: **lead weights, hook knife and flotation device**. Other than that, keep the backpack for the parachute only.

aad.title: 3. The AAD in the X-ray: cutter and battery
aad.text: The AAD (Automatic Activation Device, such as the CYPRES, the Vigil or the MarS M2) is the device that opens the reserve by itself if you are still in freefall below a safe altitude. It's what makes the officer suspicious: a small electronic box, cables and a cutter. The manufacturers publish documents to explain it.

parts.label: Parts in the X-ray
parts.cypres: Processing unit, cutter, cutter cable, cable and control unit.
parts.vigil: Main unit, cutter, cutter wire, wire and control unit.
parts.mars: Central unit, control unit, cutter, control unit cable and cutter cable.

cutter.label: Cutter
cutter.cypres: Declared *not* dangerous goods by the LBA (Germany). There are statements from BAM, DGAC (France), UK CAA, NZ CAA, TSA and CASA (Australia).
cutter.vigil: US DOT classification (ref. EX2002030123, "Not Regulated as Class 1"). The Belgian Ministry of Economy excluded the cutter from Class 1 explosives.
cutter.mars: Stainless steel cutter, with a 16-year life from manufacture. According to the manufacturer's X-ray card, no part of the device is subject to transport rules. MarS doesn't publish a transport certificate for the cutter, as CYPRES and Vigil do.

battery.label: Lithium battery
battery.cypres: 0.99 g of lithium per cell, built into the device. According to the manufacturer, it is not affected by the 2015 lithium battery rules.
battery.vigil: 2 lithium AA cells inside the device (UN3091), less than 1 g per cell and less than 2 g in total, inside the sealed metal case.
battery.mars: Internal battery, inside the central unit, made to last the device's whole life without replacement. The manual doesn't state the lithium content.

print.label: To print
print.mars: The X-Ray Card is at the end of the manual: page 41 of the [m2 multi manual](https://www.m2aad.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/manual_m2_multi_en_10_17_09_web-1.pdf) or page 35 of the [m2 manual](https://www.marsjev.com/media/cache/file/e1/manual_en_04_14_06.pdf).

aad.note: The cards show X-ray images of the AAD inside a rig, with each part numbered. It's exactly what the officer will see on the screen.
aad.sameDay: Jumped on the day you travel? **Check that the AAD is off before boarding.** If it's still on, switch it off manually.
aad.m2: **M2 owners:** since MarS doesn't publish a cutter certificate, the only paper you have to show at security is the X-Ray Card from the manual. Print it and take it with you.

docs.1: Your AAD's X-ray card (CYPRES, Vigil or MarS M2).
docs.2: The manufacturer's and authorities' statements on the cutter and the battery.
docs.4: Flying in the US: the TSA page on parachutes ("What Can I Bring?") and the TSA letter for skydivers, both pointed to by [USPA](https://www.uspa.org/traveling-with-equipment).
docs.5: The airline's sports equipment policy, if it has one.
docs.title: 4. Documents to print
docs.text: Paper in hand settles a lot of conversations. Take printed copies (and a copy on your phone):

xray.mars: MarS M2: the X-Ray Card is on page 41 of the [m2 multi manual](https://www.m2aad.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/manual_m2_multi_en_10_17_09_web-1.pdf) or page 35 of the [m2 manual](https://www.marsjev.com/media/cache/file/e1/manual_en_04_14_06.pdf)

statements.mars: MarS M2: MarS doesn't publish a cutter certificate, so take the X-Ray Card from the manual

security.title: 5. At the security checkpoint

before.1: **Secure the reserve handle**: run the chest strap over it or use a loop or cable tie, so nobody pulls it by accident. **Remember to remove it before jumping!**
before.2: Put the rig backpack in the tray on its own.
before.3: Keep the papers at hand, not at the bottom of a bag.
before.title: Before you reach the X-ray

inspection.1: Stay calm and friendly. And **no jokes** about what's in the backpack.
inspection.2: Explain what it is and show the AAD card.
inspection.3: Ask them **not to touch the handles** and offer to help.
inspection.4: If it has to be opened, ask for a space to open and close the rig. Sometimes it's enough to open the pilot chute pouch and show the bag with the packed canopy.
inspection.5: If the conversation gets stuck, ask for the **supervisor**, who usually has more training.
inspection.title: If they ask to inspect it

security.say: A simple explanation helps: "This is a sport parachute. This small box is a safety device that opens the reserve by itself in an emergency. Here is the manufacturer's card with the X-ray image. I can help open it; I only ask that you don't pull the handles."

usa.title: In the US, if there's a problem
usa.text: USPA advises asking for the supervisor and asking them to check the *Parachute Screening section of the Screening Checkpoint Standard Operating Procedure*. Write down the airport, date, time, airline, flight number and the officers' names.

security.residue: **Watch out for residue:** USPA tested rigs with AADs in explosive detectors and they didn't set them off. But everyday things can trigger the trace detector: lawn fertilizer, fireworks, gunshot residue and even hand lotion. Avoid handling them before you handle the rig.

time.title: How much extra time?
time.text: USPA suggests arriving **at least 30 minutes before** the time the airline recommends. SkyPoint says 45 minutes. ANAC says "as early as possible". When in doubt, arrive early.

gear.1: **Analog altimeter:** in the pressurized cabin it may go past the end of its scale. When you arrive, check that the needle goes back to zero.
gear.2: **Digital and audible altimeters:** switch them off for the trip and check the settings when you switch them on again. Long trips can drain the battery.
gear.3: **Helmet:** carry it in a padded case so it doesn't crack. A loose helmet is easy to lose.
gear.4: **Keep it dry:** wrap the rig in one or two garbage bags. A leaking bottle in the bag next to it can soak your reserve.
gear.title: 6. Altimeter, helmet and other gear

checklist.1: Checked the airline's rules (weight, size, sports equipment).
checklist.2: Rig alone in its own backpack, wrapped in a plastic bag.
checklist.3: Reserve handle secured (with a note to free it before the first jump).
checklist.4: Hook knife, weights and flotation device out of the carry-on.
checklist.5: AAD X-ray card and statements printed.
checklist.6: ANAC notice (Brazil) or TSA pages (US) printed.
checklist.7: AAD and digital altimeter switched off. Helmet in its case.
checklist.8: Arriving at the airport with at least 30 to 45 extra minutes.
checklist.9: If jumping outside Brazil: reserve repack in date and the insurance the dropzone requires.
checklist.title: 7. Checklist before leaving home

sources.1: ANAC: [Informativo SIA 29/20, carrying parachute equipment as carry-on (in Portuguese)](https://www.gov.br/anac/pt-br/centrais-de-conteudo/aeroportos-e-aerodromos/informativos-sia/2020-29)
